clinicalPearls: Torsion of the appendix testis is a common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys and is a self-limiting, benign condition, in contrast to testicular torsion
The classic sign is a small tender nodule at the upper pole of the testis with a bluish discolouration visible through the scrotal skin, the blue-dot sign
Pain tends to be more gradual and less severe than in testicular torsion, and the testis itself usually lies in a normal vertical position with a preserved cremasteric reflex
The key clinical priority is to exclude testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency, and diagnostic uncertainty should prompt scrotal exploration
Colour Doppler scrotal ultrasound typically shows normal or increased testicular blood flow with a non-vascular tender appendage, supporting the diagnosis
Management is usually conservative with rest, scrotal support, and simple analgesia, as symptoms settle over days as the appendage infarcts and involutes
Surgical excision of the twisted appendage is reserved for severe or persistent pain or when torsion cannot be excluded
reference.pathophysiology: The appendix testis is a small pedunculated Mullerian duct remnant at the upper pole of the testis. Its narrow stalk predisposes it to twisting, which cuts off its blood supply and causes ischaemia and infarction of the appendage. The resulting inflammation produces localised pain and tenderness, and the infarcted appendage may be visible as a bluish nodule beneath the scrotal skin. Because the testis itself is not compromised, the process is self-limiting and resolves as the appendage necroses and is reabsorbed.
additionalInvestigations: Careful clinical examination for the blue-dot sign, testicular lie, and cremasteric reflex
Colour Doppler scrotal ultrasound to confirm preserved testicular perfusion
Scrotal exploration when testicular torsion cannot be reliably excluded
redFlags: Sudden severe pain, high-riding or transversely lying testis, or absent cremasteric reflex suggesting testicular torsion
Reduced or absent testicular blood flow on Doppler
Diagnostic uncertainty in a boy with an acute scrotum
Systemic features raising concern for another surgical or infective cause
reference.prognosis: Torsion of the appendix testis is benign and self-limiting; symptoms typically resolve within one to two weeks with conservative care and there is no threat to testicular viability or future fertility.
pitfalls: Attributing an acute scrotum to appendage torsion and missing testicular torsion
Relying on ultrasound to exclude torsion when clinical suspicion is high, rather than exploring
Over-diagnosing epididymo-orchitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics
Failing to reassess a boy whose pain worsens or fails to settle
management: Exclude testicular torsion urgently, proceeding to scrotal exploration whenever it cannot be reliably ruled out
Confirm preserved testicular perfusion with colour Doppler ultrasound when the diagnosis is suggested clinically by a blue-dot sign
Conservative management with rest, scrotal support, and simple analgesia such as an NSAID once torsion is excluded
Reassure that the condition is benign and self-limiting as the appendage infarcts and involutes over days to weeks
Surgical excision of the twisted appendage for severe or persistent pain not settling with conservative care
Clinical follow-up to confirm symptom resolution and reassess if pain worsens
